findings.title: The stuck model's advantage depends on the generator
findings.text: Hazard, benefits-processor, generators we wrote (120 generated people per v2 cell; the v1 generator has 4 personas): the v1 stuck model beats time-since-progress by 0.071 nats per bin on its own generator, and the advantage falls to 0.008 to 0.015 on three harder generator families. A v1-trained model is 0.43 to 0.53 nats worse than the baseline on their data (H1 -0.43 to -0.53). False alarms: the interval is entirely above the 1.0 per hour budget in 3 of 6 v2-to-v2 off-diagonal cells, 1 of 3 v2 diagonals, 3 of 3 v1-to-v2 cells and 0 of 3 v2-to-v1 cells. Cells with no skill (the H1 interval includes zero or lies below it): latent_skill->markov, latent_skill->process_trace, v1->latent_skill, v1->markov, v1->process_trace. The v1 headline (log loss 0.436 against 0.509 for time since progress, leave one person out, on the four v1 personas) therefore largely reflects the generator's emission table; it stays labelled as a generator result.

findings.title: The language-model study cannot show an effect: the outcome sits at the floor
findings.text: Language-model participants, not people. Run 4 (n = 24: 16 coached-arm and 8 A/A participants): 30 of 32 coached post-tests scored 0 (the floor) and 16 of 16 A/A post-tests; the action cap was hit in 18 of 32 coached post-tests. The headline difference is +0.094 [-0.051, +0.239], sign-flip p = 0.5. An outcome at the floor means a null shows nothing: it does not show the coach has no effect. With 16 coached-arm participants the analysis has about 6% false positives and 12%, 29% and 76% power for a small, medium and large true effect (engine-analytics Monte Carlo, interval excludes zero); sign-flip p below 0.05 has less. A null or small result does not show that the coach has no effect; a result counts as clear only if the interval excludes zero. Run 5 pilot: 0 of 6 post-tests scored above zero (needed 3); stopped, so there is no run 5 proper (reason recorded: only 0 of 6 pilot post-tests scored above zero (needed 3)). Study-mode enforcement held: 0 non-silent coach polls in post-test blocks and 0 in blocks with the coach off (including A/A); 12 nudges were shown, all in train blocks.

reasons_for_stopping: only 0 of 6 pilot post-tests scored above zero (needed 3)

findings.title: ML v2 does not transfer to the language-model participants
findings.text: M5, out-of-generator transfer (language-model participants, not people; test only, no decision rule; n = 24 participants, 419 scored 30 s bins): neither v1 nor v2 transfers to the floor-bound behaviour of those traces. Log loss is 1.43 [1.25 to 1.60] for v1 and 1.46 [1.31 to 1.61] for v2 against 1.08 [1.00 to 1.15] for the base rate, and calibration is destroyed (expected calibration error 0.51 [0.45 to 0.57] and 0.53 [0.47 to 0.58]). The label shifts: 65% of the test bins are 'stuck' against 22% in training, because progress is sparse in these traces. v2 minus v1 log loss is +0.030 with an interval of -0.030 to 0.085: no improvement. Reported as is; the models and alarm rules were fixed before these traces existed.

findings.title: Deficit detection does not hold up on harder generators
findings.text: Genome (deficit detection), benefits-processor, generators we wrote (16 personas on the v1 generator, 87 to 92 generated people per v2 cell): precision 92% and recall 95% on the v1 generator fall to 48 to 71% precision and 49 to 68% recall on three harder generator families (thresholds fitted and tested on the same family). Thresholds fitted on v1 keep recall (87 to 95%) but lose precision (33 to 56%); thresholds fitted on a v2 family give v1 high precision (79 to 100%) but recall of only 10 to 42%. False attribution to deficits that are absent is 46 to 59 s on the v2 families against 1.1 s on v1. The v1 figures describe the v1 generator, not workers.

findings.title: The repeat finder's precision depends on the generator; the gate carries the proposals
findings.text: Routines (repeat finder, then the proposal gate), benefits-processor, generators we wrote (4 personas on the v1 generator, 120 generated people per v2 cell; shipped thresholds, which do not depend on the fit family): raw cluster precision is 22% on the v1 generator (the published figure) and 44 to 97% on the three v2 families, with recall 45 to 92% (100% on v1). Proposal precision after the gate is 74 to 100% (100% on v1). Thresholds fitted per family transfer unevenly: across the fitted off-diagonal cells raw precision ranges from 4 to 100% and recall from 16 to 100%. The two thin roles (data-analyst, programmer; v2 families only, shipped thresholds) give raw precision 88 to 98%, recall 60 to 92% and proposal precision 100%, so the figures differ by role as well as by family. These numbers say how many of the clusters found are real routines in a generator we wrote, not in real workers.

findings.title: ML v2 expert-envelope and counterfactual candidates (E4, Q1) are rejected
findings.text: ML v2 genome families on the held-out apprentice cohort (6 cohorts, 96 novices; all generated): the pre-registered primary candidates E4 (expert envelope) and Q1 (counterfactual price) are both harmful and so rejected. The primary metric is the mean absolute error, in seconds, of the recovered price of a deficit, paired against v1's attribution, so a positive difference is worse: E4 +3.81 [+2.30, +5.19] s, Q1 +1.17 [+0.44, +1.87] s. Other E variants: E1 accepted (-0.92 [-1.85, -0.21] s), E2 null (+0.00 [+0.00, +0.00] s), E3 harmful (+4.57 [+3.14, +6.01] s). v1's attribution stays the default for these families. Reported as is: the candidates were frozen before the held-out run.

findings.title: Under generator mismatch the time-since-progress baseline beats v1
findings.text: ML v2 under generator mismatch (fit on one generator family, test on another; pooled off-diagonal cells; all generated): the plain time-since-progress baseline beats v1 on log loss, paired against v1 (negative is better; adjusted intervals as recorded): benefits-processor -0.021 [-0.034, -0.010]; data-analyst -0.024 [-0.034, -0.014]; programmer -0.030 [-0.041, -0.019]. The accepted v2 (A4) improves on v1 by -0.014 [-0.019, -0.009] for benefits-processor under the same test, a smaller improvement than the baseline's, so on this test a rule that only counts time since progress does better than the accepted v2 when the generator changes. The held-out result is reported as is; it is about our generators, not about workers.

limitations.text: The planner is a script that follows any instruction it can see. These numbers measure what the layers stop, not how a real model behaves under attack.
Attacks are scripted and were written by the same team that wrote the defences. A new attack style can get through.
Layer 1 (sanitising) is modelled as defeating only markup-based attacks (fake system tags, tool-call syntax); a scripted planner that follows plain text shows no change when it is off.
Layers overlap, so leaving one out often changes nothing. The 'only_<layer>' rows show each layer's standalone strength.
A detector hit pauses the run for a human, so task success under attack is lower than on clean pages by design.

Removing the injection detector did not let any attack through in this test, but it lets far more tasks finish (the reader alone keeps the planner clean). The detector's job is to catch an attack early, and its price is pauses.

Layer 7 (goal check) no longer asks a model about plain typing, filling, select and extract steps, so it now covers navigation, clicks and key presses only. We changed this after seeing it pause the run on clean pages when the worker was just typing the answer (5 false pauses in 93 live runs). The false-pause figure after the change (0 of 93) is measured on the same pages that showed the problem, so it is in-sample and probably too good; typed data is still stopped by the data-flow and action-gate layers, not by this one.

Data-flow rules and the goal check cannot tell an exfiltration request to an endpoint on a site the routine already uses from normal browsing there. Only the detector and the reader stop that kind of attack.

caveats.text: A screen frame is raw content. The guard decides whether a frame may leave, from which kind of source, what may come back and what is ever recorded; it does not redact or generalise pixels, and when a frame is allowed the provider sees everything on the screen. What a provider does with a frame it received is the provider's policy and is not measured here.
Closed answer schemas (every string is an enum) stop text read off the screen from coming back. They cannot stop the model from seeing it.

A frame is held in a buffer that is wiped after the call and is never written by this layer. Copies handed to a provider SDK or the HTTP stack, and freed memory the interpreter has not reused, cannot be wiped or controlled from here; swap and core dumps are outside this check.

The residue scan looks for the planted PNG's raw bytes, the token written into its metadata, its full SHA-256, and base64 or hex renderings of the file. It cannot see pixels, a re-encoded copy (a JPEG of the same frame), or a description of the frame.

The gate is a pure function of four booleans and a source that the caller computes. The guard cannot check that secure input or a denylisted app was detected correctly, or that a frame really came from the source it declares.

limitations.text: The canary scan looks for the exact planted strings, their invented words, simple rewrites (case, separators, URL encoding, base64, hex). A paraphrase, a translation, a hash or a character-code encoding of a token would not be caught. The claim measured is: these planted strings did not reach the model port, in these flows.

The leak bound is read per RUN, not per token. A leak is a property of a code path, and the many tokens planted in one run share that path, so they are not independent trials. With 0 leaks the one-sided 95% upper bound is about 3 divided by the number of independent units: per run (for example 0 of 80) about 3.7%, per flow (0 of 10) about 26%; the token-level figure (0 of thousands, well under 0.1%) assumes independence that does not hold and is shown only for comparison. Eight seeds per flow vary the planted strings, not the code path, so more seeds do not shrink the per-flow bound.

Reference flows test the privacy layer with stand-in upstream code. Only integration flows test another layer's own code, and a layer that supplied none is listed as none_registered, not as passed. Zero leaks says nothing about a flow that was not run.

A SafePayload limits the form of what is sent (numbers, codes, fixed ids, bucketed values), not its meaning: a bucketed count of the worker's own meetings is still a fact about the worker. Generalisation reduces precision; it is not anonymisation.

Lists of integers could carry text as character codes. Lists are capped at 64 items and integers at 1e9, which bounds that; the threat model is accidental leakage by honest code, not an author trying to smuggle data out.

git.statement: No real people are involved. Every developer in the habit, placebo, digest and canary results is a scripted persona (4 learners and 8 experts per replicate) and every commit message is generated text. limitations.text: Every learner and expert is a scripted persona. Recovering planted habits shows that the features, the thresholds and the intervals work on data built to contain them; it says nothing about how real developers behave.

The generator, the digest rules and the habit thresholds were written by the same agent. Thresholds were set on development replicates 0 to 3 and scored on fresh ones (100 and up), but the planted rates are large and habits are planted independently; real habits are smaller, correlated and noisier.
Small differences are not flagged by design (each habit has a floor). At 25% of the planted strength recall falls to 19%.
Reverts are rare even when planted, so the revert habit is the weakest to recover; it is reported, not tuned.
Evaluation digests come from the rules, because model digests take about a second a commit. The local model was not present, so model-against-rules agreement was not measured.

On commit sessions the alignment sees differences in the SHAPE of sessions (missing test steps, reverts, extra code-commit loops) in some replicates, and sees nothing in seconds, because git records when a commit landed and not how long the work took. Habits that live in the message or the clock (vague messages, late nights) are invisible to cogs by construction.
Suggestions are advice chosen by code from commit-level shares. Nobody has been shown that following one improves anything; there is no study of the git layer, and a share is not a cause.
A real repository is compared with generated experts, so its origin is reported as mixed; the comparison is with a scripted baseline, not with real experts.
The one real history (this project's) is short and agent-assisted; its aggregates illustrate the pipeline and are not a finding.
The leak result is a count of exact planted strings in captured request bodies on these flows. It does not catch a paraphrase, a translation or a hash of a token.

limitations.text: Every figure for the proactive layer comes from generated personas, learners and git learners with planted structure we wrote. It shows that the judge, verify and prepare steps recover what was planted, not that real workers would find these cards useful.

The definition of 'worth surfacing' is ours and was fixed before the runs (see the output). For the personas, the planted skill is mapped to a level and fed to both the gate and the truth, so agreement on practice cards for personas is partly built in; the learner and git truths are more independent of the code under test.

The truth definitions and one part of the practice scoring were revised after looking at the first replays (listed under design.truth_revisions and design.code_revision, with the first-run figures). There is no held-out data: the reported precision and recall are development-set figures on the same generated personas and learners, and are optimistic for that reason.

The ranking weights, the minimum score of 0.30, the cap of three and the per-kind limits are hand-set constants, not fitted to any data. A different choice would move precision and recall; no sensitivity sweep is claimed.

There are 4 personas, 3 learners and 4 git learners, with several decision points each. Decision points inside one person are correlated, so the pooled Wilson intervals are too narrow; the person-level bootstrap is the honest interval and it is wide.

Recall is capped at what the judge is allowed to show of each kind (one practice card, one git card, two automations): a person with three planted git habits is credited for finding one. That is the design, not a flaw in the metric, but it hides how much was left unsaid.

Calendar cards are scored against the calendar track's planted problems; the suggestion thresholds and the planted structure come from the same generator family, and a week can carry several planted problems of which the judge may show one. Finished-run cards are covered by scripted checks only, and so are stale calendar and git cards.

Acceptance learning is shown on a generated worker with fixed rates. It has not been validated on people, and a real person's accepts and declines may depend on time of day, mood and the card's wording, none of which are modelled.
No model decides what is surfaced; a model may reword the reason line through the egress guard. Wording quality is not evaluated here.

Staleness is injected by changing a reading (a routine switched on, a skill at level 4). Real staleness has more forms, and a source that cannot be read is never treated as stale, which can leave a card up for a few hours after it stopped being true.

limitations.text: Every calendar number is on generated calendars with planted structure (4 personas, 8 experts, 16 novices, 3 weeks). Nothing about the calendar layer is validated on real people, and one read-only aggregate check of the owner's own calendar says nothing about anyone else.

The expert reference is generated from the role template that also defines the targets, so agreement with it is by construction. The template is hand-authored, not measured on real experts, and real experts differ by person, team and week.

Event kinds (meeting, focus, break, off-screen) come from keyword rules on titles and attendee counts. Real titles are messier; a meeting with no invitees is read as the owner's own time, and a focus block that is not named as one is invisible. Calendar hygiene differs from how people really work.

A problem planted below the expert tolerance (one fragmented day, one back-to-back run) is not suggested, by design. Recall against the planted intent is therefore below 1; the thresholds come from the template, not from the truth labels.

Gap intervals cover uncertainty in the expert reference (8 generated experts) only, not a learner's week-to-week variation; a week is flagged only if it also lies outside the range of expert weeks. Three weeks per person is thin.

The Microsoft Graph adapters were tested against recorded fake responses written from the public documentation; they have never been run against a live tenant by this code, and tenant policy decides what a signed-in worker may read.

The leak result is measured: the exact planted names, addresses, titles, locations and ids did not appear in any payload, suggestion or captured request. It does not rule out a paraphrase or an encoding, and model calls the worker asks for are recorded in the egress ledger, not hidden.

limitations.text: Every digest number is measured on generated commits and calendar entries with planted labels, written by the same author as the rules and the prompts. No real repository, calendar or person was used; accuracy on real data is unknown and probably lower.

About 100 items per task in the held-out test split (and 50 in the dev split the prompts were tuned on): the Wilson intervals are wide, and differences of a few points between the model and the rules are not distinguishable.

The prompt wording, the worked examples and the per-field choice of model or rules were tuned on the dev split only; the held-out test split was run once with the frozen prompts (one later look at the shipped-policy arm followed the single policy revision, see loc_policy_revised). Dev numbers are therefore optimistic and are shown only as such.

No fine-tuning (LOC-3 is cut): it could not be validated in the time available. The model is Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct at 4-bit quantisation (Q4_K_M) with a labelling guide, a few fixed worked examples and constrained decoding.
Labels such as risk and message quality are our written policy, not ground truth: a reviewer may reasonably disagree on a share of items, which caps the accuracy any method can show here.

Size, tests touched, duration, attendee count and recurrence are computed by code from the input in every path, so they are exact by construction and say nothing about the model; only category, risk, message quality and needs_prep are model-or-rules fields.

Small prompt changes move the numbers by more than the intervals suggest: replacing three worked examples (to keep them disjoint from the fixtures) changed dev commit-category accuracy from 48 to 44 of 52. A difference of a few items between two prompts or between the model and the rules is noise at this sample size.

The rules, the labelling policy, the prompts' guide and the fixture generator share one author and one vocabulary (for example the list of sensitive areas), so the rules are better matched to these fixtures than they would be to real history, and the model's labelling guide is better matched than it would be to real history. Real data would test both.

'No leak' is claimed only as measured: zero planted strings in the outputs and in the server log of the evaluation run, and the guards reject a deliberately leaking stand-in model. The raw inputs do pass through the local model's memory and llama.cpp's in-process prompt cache (never written to disk by this module).

Latency and tokens per second are for one Apple M2 Max (32 GB) with all layers on the GPU: about 30 generated tokens per second, so a digest takes roughly 0.5 s when only the category is asked for (the shipped policy) and about 0.7 to 1.1 s with every field. A history of a thousand commits takes about nine minutes the first time; the rules path takes microseconds.

Constrained decoding means an instruction planted in the input cannot make the model print text: nothing leaves a digest except vocabulary values. It can still steer labels. With one planted line on 20 items per task, the model-for-everything run moved to the value the line asked for in 19 of 19 (commit category revert), 17 of 17 (risk high), 13 of 17 (event category focus) and 12 of 12 (needs_prep true); the keyword rules moved in 0, 0, 0 and 0. In the shipped policy only category is model-decided, and code vetoes the two most consequential claims (a revert needs a revert-style message; focus time needs at most one attendee), which leaves 0 of 19 and 5 of 17 category steerings; other category values can still be steered by whoever writes the commit message or the invite.

Which fields the model decides was chosen on the dev split and revised once after the held-out run (events needs_prep moved from the model to the rules). The held-out numbers of the model-for-everything run are the clean evidence; the numbers for the policy as shipped (commit_digest: category, event_digest: category by the model) include one held-out look after that revision and are slightly optimistic.

run_python uses macOS sandbox-exec (deprecated by Apple but present) and fails closed without it. Memory is bounded by a resident-size watchdog polled every 250 ms, not a kernel limit (macOS refuses RLIMIT_AS).
Injection detection is a rule set. The planted strings are of the styles the rules cover, so the detection rate here is an upper bound.
The nightly replay uses a fake screen and a stand-in presence service; it checks the decision flow, not the real lock screen or forecast.
Latencies were measured on a development laptop shared with other processes; treat them as indicative.

The long-horizon bugs are single-token mutations of correct code (an operator, a boundary, a constant), repaired by fault localisation plus mutation search over three classes, the standard way to test repair tools. Success shows the loop, the rollback, the verification and the privacy path work over 14 steps; it does not show the runtime fixes arbitrary bugs. The data task has three planted problem types and one reconciliation target; the outlier rule (50 times the median) is the same in the engine and in the checker.

Offline long-horizon runs use a deterministic stand-in for the model that reads the same typed payload (typed history and typed signals) and follows the playbook; it shows the loop is closed and adaptive, not that a language model would choose the same steps. The live smoke measures that with the real model on the same tasks, with its own n.

A script that exits non-zero is recoverable up to three times (the child retries or changes course); any blocker (timeout, escape attempt, injection hit) or uncertain check still stops the child for a human at once.

The refactor exemplar makes one narrow, behaviour-preserving change (a repeated number becomes a named constant), verified by applying it to a fresh copy and running the tests. It does not claim general refactoring ability.

limitations.text: Every number in this section comes from generated people or language-model participants, not people. A gain on generated data can be the model learning the generator; held-out replicates share the generator and cannot rule that out.

The held-out persona and apprentice replicates are fresh seeds of the same generators: they catch overfitting to one noise draw, not learning the generator. Only the cross-family matrix (three differently built generators, still written by us) and the language-model participant traces go beyond it.
The awareness features come from a generator that plants a cursor-to-stuck link by assumption; an ablation lift shows the pipeline can use a planted signal, not that real cursors predict being stuck.

The risk-controlled alarm threshold is guaranteed only for exchangeable episodes and independent false alarms; it fails for a new person who differs from the training people, for drift and for clustered alarms.

The seconds-if-fixed estimate assumes the rest of the path would be unchanged. It fails when habits interact; the generator's prices are additive by construction, so the stress test with a planted interaction is invented by us.

The deficit rows that stay mis-priced (copy error, repeated reads) are mis-priced by the rule that names alignment columns after the alignment, not by the substitution costs; a better labelling rule written from our own planted structure would be fitting the generator, so none was added.
The language-model participant traces have few progress events and short cases, so the transfer numbers rest on little and the label is nearly constant; the test is reported whatever it shows.

finding.title: ML v2 does not transfer to the language-model participants
finding.text: M5, out-of-generator transfer (language-model participants, not people; test only, no decision rule; n = 24 participants, 419 scored 30 s bins): neither v1 nor v2 transfers to the floor-bound behaviour of those traces. Log loss is 1.43 [1.25 to 1.60] for v1 and 1.46 [1.31 to 1.61] for v2 against 1.08 [1.00 to 1.15] for the base rate, and calibration is destroyed (expected calibration error 0.51 [0.45 to 0.57] and 0.53 [0.47 to 0.58]). The label shifts: 65% of the test bins are 'stuck' against 22% in training, because progress is sparse in these traces. v2 minus v1 log loss is +0.030 with an interval of -0.030 to 0.085: no improvement. Reported as is; the models and alarm rules were fixed before these traces existed.

more_findings.title: ML v2 expert-envelope and counterfactual candidates (E4, Q1) are rejected
more_findings.text: ML v2 genome families on the held-out apprentice cohort (6 cohorts, 96 novices; all generated): the pre-registered primary candidates E4 (expert envelope) and Q1 (counterfactual price) are both harmful and so rejected. The primary metric is the mean absolute error, in seconds, of the recovered price of a deficit, paired against v1's attribution, so a positive difference is worse: E4 +3.81 [+2.30, +5.19] s, Q1 +1.17 [+0.44, +1.87] s. Other E variants: E1 accepted (-0.92 [-1.85, -0.21] s), E2 null (+0.00 [+0.00, +0.00] s), E3 harmful (+4.57 [+3.14, +6.01] s). v1's attribution stays the default for these families. Reported as is: the candidates were frozen before the held-out run.

more_findings.title: Under generator mismatch the time-since-progress baseline beats v1
more_findings.text: ML v2 under generator mismatch (fit on one generator family, test on another; pooled off-diagonal cells; all generated): the plain time-since-progress baseline beats v1 on log loss, paired against v1 (negative is better; adjusted intervals as recorded): benefits-processor -0.021 [-0.034, -0.010]; data-analyst -0.024 [-0.034, -0.014]; programmer -0.030 [-0.041, -0.019]. The accepted v2 (A4) improves on v1 by -0.014 [-0.019, -0.009] for benefits-processor under the same test, a smaller improvement than the baseline's, so on this test a rule that only counts time since progress does better than the accepted v2 when the generator changes. The held-out result is reported as is; it is about our generators, not about workers.

limitations.text: The explainer improves readability, not accuracy. A faithful-sounding explanation can still rest on a wrong number: the check proves each number traces to a field of the packet, not that the packet is true.

The false-reject rate is measured on a stand-in model that varies numbers and interval wording in the ways we wrote down. A real model phrases things we did not anticipate, so its false-reject rate is likely higher; a rejected reply costs nothing (the template is used).

The adversarial rejection rate is against the 29 attacks we wrote. The unknown-habit rule is a set of cue patterns (a cause or a share of time attributed to a phrase that names nothing in the vocabulary), not a language model: a novel phrasing with no cue can pass.

Packets come from scripted apprentices (and the real stuck-hazard evaluation in the full run); the coach, routine, counterfactual and time-to-progress blocks are scripted fixtures that exercise wording and the check, not measurements.

The deterministic template is the shipped wording: it passes its own check on every packet and every intent, with no model. A model's words are used only when they pass the same check, and how often they do depends on the model and the mode (live, small n, real models, 7 Nov 2026): local Qwen2.5-7B composing freely 1 of 30; rewording a code-written draft 12 of 30 [24.6%, 57.7%] then, after the hedge and wording fixes, 24 of 30 [62.7%, 90.5%]; cloud gpt-5.4-mini composing from the packet 0 of 13 [0%, 22.8%]; cloud gemini-3.5-flash-lite 7 of 9 [45.3%, 93.7%] (see live.recorded). The model layer improves readability only when it passes the check, so the default text says 'words from the template'.
The live block, when it is run, is a small-n pass rate for one local model on generated packets; it says nothing about other models.

Grounding is a fake port right at a chosen rate. Real accuracy on real screens is not measured here; the 60 to 100% sweep is a what-if.

The composite overstates mastery for learners who do not improve and rises 10 points or more in about a third of them. It is experimental and in no headline; independence and the trend are the evidence, and the trend has low power.
A learner who dismisses a cue and then grinds through alone looks independent in the ledger; the guards remove dismiss-and-walk-away and implicit follows within 10 s but cannot remove that leak.
Candidate accuracy is measured on 8 scripted apprentice experts and on experts sampled from the pack's own rules; real experts will do things neither contains.

finding.title: The stuck model's advantage depends on the generator
finding.text: Hazard, benefits-processor, generators we wrote (120 generated people per v2 cell; the v1 generator has 4 personas): the v1 stuck model beats time-since-progress by 0.071 nats per bin on its own generator, and the advantage falls to 0.008 to 0.015 on three harder generator families. A v1-trained model is 0.43 to 0.53 nats worse than the baseline on their data (H1 -0.43 to -0.53). False alarms: the interval is entirely above the 1.0 per hour budget in 3 of 6 v2-to-v2 off-diagonal cells, 1 of 3 v2 diagonals, 3 of 3 v1-to-v2 cells and 0 of 3 v2-to-v1 cells. Cells with no skill (the H1 interval includes zero or lies below it): latent_skill->markov, latent_skill->process_trace, v1->latent_skill, v1->markov, v1->process_trace. The v1 headline (log loss 0.436 against 0.509 for time since progress, leave one person out, on the four v1 personas) therefore largely reflects the generator's emission table; it stays labelled as a generator result.

more_findings.title: Deficit detection does not hold up on harder generators
more_findings.text: Genome (deficit detection), benefits-processor, generators we wrote (16 personas on the v1 generator, 87 to 92 generated people per v2 cell): precision 92% and recall 95% on the v1 generator fall to 48 to 71% precision and 49 to 68% recall on three harder generator families (thresholds fitted and tested on the same family). Thresholds fitted on v1 keep recall (87 to 95%) but lose precision (33 to 56%); thresholds fitted on a v2 family give v1 high precision (79 to 100%) but recall of only 10 to 42%. False attribution to deficits that are absent is 46 to 59 s on the v2 families against 1.1 s on v1. The v1 figures describe the v1 generator, not workers.

more_findings.title: The repeat finder's precision depends on the generator; the gate carries the proposals
more_findings.text: Routines (repeat finder, then the proposal gate), benefits-processor, generators we wrote (4 personas on the v1 generator, 120 generated people per v2 cell; shipped thresholds, which do not depend on the fit family): raw cluster precision is 22% on the v1 generator (the published figure) and 44 to 97% on the three v2 families, with recall 45 to 92% (100% on v1). Proposal precision after the gate is 74 to 100% (100% on v1). Thresholds fitted per family transfer unevenly: across the fitted off-diagonal cells raw precision ranges from 4 to 100% and recall from 16 to 100%. The two thin roles (data-analyst, programmer; v2 families only, shipped thresholds) give raw precision 88 to 98%, recall 60 to 92% and proposal precision 100%, so the figures differ by role as well as by family. These numbers say how many of the clusters found are real routines in a generator we wrote, not in real workers.

limitations.text: Language-model participants, not people: The participants are language-model agents, not people. Nothing here shows that people learn from the coach, and nothing here is a user study.

Language-model participants, not people: The only 'memory' a participant has is a note of at most 280 characters that it wrote itself after the practice case and sees again at the post-test of the same skill. Every case starts from a fresh model context. That is a prompt, not learning in any human sense.

Language-model participants, not people: A model that is shown 'check cliff edges before you copy this result' can do what it says. A higher score after coaching can therefore be instruction following plus a self-written note, not retention of a skill.
Language-model participants, not people: The coach prompts, the sandbox sites, the households, the scoring rule and the personas were all written by us.

Language-model participants, not people: With 16 coached-arm participants the analysis has about 6% false positives and 12%, 29% and 76% power for a small, medium and large true effect (engine-analytics Monte Carlo, interval excludes zero); sign-flip p below 0.05 has less. A null or small result does not show that the coach has no effect; a result counts as clear only if the interval excludes zero.

Language-model participants, not people: The counterbalanced design cancels a fixed block-2 shift and generic carry-over, not spill-over of the coached gain to the other skill in block 2, which dilutes the contrast. Because each block starts from a fresh model context, order and fatigue effects are absent by construction.

Language-model participants, not people: Timing is not human. Each action is followed by a fixed 2 s pause and the model's own latency varies, so effort is reported as ACTION COUNTS and the coach's poll-to-prompt delay is a property of the pipeline, not of people. A fast participant can finish the note page before a prompt arrives.

Language-model participants, not people: The coach is real but the overlay renderer is a stand-in: a ring is drawn only when an element carrying the target zone exists on the page the participant is on. The cliff button exists only on a calculator result tab, not on the case note page where the prompt usually arrives. The reconcile target was `results_tabs` (no page element) when the plan was written; the pipeline snapshot used targets `reconcile_control` (the case note's dropdown), which exists. The by-zone table shows which was served.

Language-model participants, not people: Participants are reached through the shared model port's fast-tier check call, whose fixed instructions tell the model to treat quoted material as data. That may make it less responsive to on-page text in both arms.

Language-model participants, not people: The build machine was heavily loaded by other agents' tests while the participants ran (1-minute load average above 100 on 12 CPUs, sampled and reported), so wall-clock times, the coach's 3 s polls, the extension's event flush and the prompt delays are slower and noisier than on an idle machine. needed_difference_n4.rule: the 95% t interval (df = 3) excludes 0 only when the mean of the four differences exceeds 1.591 x the standard deviation of those four differences

needed_difference_n4.reading: Of all 625 possible sets of four differences, only 16 (2.6%) put the interval above 0: every one of the four differences must be at least 0.5 (half a point on the 0-to-1 scale), and with any spread the mean must be at least 0.625. In the simulation the typical spread of the four differences is about 0.50, which would need a mean of about 0.80. Only a very large effect, seen in every participant, can show.

study_power.note: Monte Carlo of the pre-registered analysis (10000 replications per cell, seed 20261107) on the exactly counterbalanced design. At n = 4 the smallest attainable two-sided sign-flip p is 0.125, so p < 0.05 is impossible (power_p05 = 0 in every n = 4 cell). With no nuisance, the t-interval power at n = 4 is 1.7% at no effect (false positives), 2.4% / 4.4% / 11.6% at a 10 / 21 / 39 point effect; at n = 24 it is 5.1%, 12.9%, 39.1%, 91.1%. This shows what the design could detect under our assumptions, not that the effect exists.

limitations.text: Hazard, skills, policy, routing and agent-claim results come from generated personas, scripted apprentices or simulators we wrote. They show that the methods recover structure we planted, not that real workers behave this way.

The study power analysis only shows what the planned design could detect under assumptions we made up (how much people differ, how big the training gain is, how carry-over and fatigue behave). It does not show that an effect exists, and with four people no result can reach p below 0.05.

With four teammates the exact two-sided sign-flip p cannot go below 0.125, and the interval excludes zero only when the four differences nearly agree and are large. The expected outcome is an interval that includes zero.

caveats: Every number depends on invented assumptions: baseline propensities, how much people differ, the size of the training gain, independent checks within a case, and the form of carry-over and fatigue. The sensitivity block varies the first four.
The estimand is the direct coaching gain averaged over the two skills; carry-over that spills the coached gain onto the other skill dilutes the contrast and the design cannot cancel it (see bias).

A balanced design cancels a fixed block-2 shift and generic carry-over in expectation, which is why false positives stay near the nominal rate when the true effect is 0; it adds variance, which costs power.

The plan's t interval is not exact for discrete bounded scores, and it has zero width when all differences are identical; coverage and the false-positive rate are reported from simulation, with Monte Carlo intervals.
Real participants are four teammates who know the project; demand effects and facilitator bias are not in this model.
