limitations.text: Almost every result in this report comes from scripted apprentices, generated personas or simulators we wrote; each section says what it was measured on. They show that the methods recover the structure we planted, not that real workers behave this way.

The live study has n = 4, all teammates, none of them benefits processors (planned; it has not been run). Intervals are wide and the result is a case study. The headline measure is unassisted performance on a later matched task, reported separately from assisted speed.

Real data is thin: the only real signal is the team's own machine timestamps (times only, collected with consent). There are no real benefits-processor traces, so nothing here has been validated on real casework.

The entitlement figures the agent is scored against come from a simplified internal rule set, not the law. It agrees with PolicyEngine UK within 1 pound on only 8 of 20 generated households, so passing our oracle is not the same as getting the entitlement right.
The stuck hazard is evaluated on four generated personas, so 'held-out person' means one of four. Intervals resample episodes, not people; the per-person spread is the honest uncertainty.

Review routing is grounded in sandbox households scored by calculators whose quirks we planted, against a simplified internal reference rather than law. The router finding those quirks shows it recovers our planted structure, not that real calculators or real agents fail this way; the task is nearly deterministic, and the plain spread of calculator answers does almost as well.

The routing error bound holds for cases like the ones used to calibrate it. A new benefit rule, calculator site or household type breaks that assumption silently. Review time per case is an assumption.

Ski-rental regret is measured on generated routines (lognormal run rates, 45% retiring after an exponential life, the forecast sees 10 workdays), not on real build decisions. It shows the rule's behaviour against break-even under a stated mechanism.

The only real agent traces so far are 68 claimed successes from 20 households on the sandbox sites, from one real model. All 20 false claims are one family of failure: the model said it was done on a one-off error page. A classifier can mostly learn 'this was an error page', which a one-line rule also catches, so this does not show that claim risk can be predicted in general.
The planner is a script that follows any instruction it can see. These numbers measure what the layers stop, not how a real model behaves under attack.

Each attack is run 3 times per configuration on a catalog of a few dozen scripted attacks. Repeats of one attack are not independent evidence (the intervals are clustered by attack); intervals are wide and the point estimates are not rates to rely on.

The leak bound is read per RUN, not per token. A leak is a property of a code path, and the many tokens planted in one run share that path, so they are not independent trials. With 0 leaks the one-sided 95% upper bound is about 3 divided by the number of independent units: per run (for example 0 of 80) about 3.7%, per flow (0 of 10) about 26%; the token-level figure (0 of thousands, well under 0.1%) assumes independence that does not hold and is shown only for comparison. Eight seeds per flow vary the planted strings, not the code path, so more seeds do not shrink the per-flow bound.

Reference flows test the privacy layer with stand-in upstream code. Only integration flows test another layer's own code, and a layer that supplied none is listed as none_registered, not as passed. Zero leaks says nothing about a flow that was not run.

A screen frame is raw content. The guard decides whether a frame may leave, from which kind of source, what may come back and what is ever recorded; it does not redact or generalise pixels, and when a frame is allowed the provider sees everything on the screen. What a provider does with a frame it received is the provider's policy and is not measured here.

The gate is a pure function of four booleans and a source that the caller computes. The guard cannot check that secure input or a denylisted app was detected correctly, or that a frame really came from the source it declares.

ENFORCED: the Python awareness package and the awareness, Live and hotkey TypeScript may not contain the string 'sandbox' (static scan, test files skipped); the frame route can refuse another machine, an unknown source, and a sandbox claim from a web page whose Origin is not one of our sandbox sites (frame_request_problem). BY CONVENTION ONLY: a local process on this Mac sends no Origin header, so the route cannot tell the Electron main process from the agent service; a local process that wrongly declares sandbox is not stopped, only visible in the ledger's source column.

Every learner and expert is a scripted persona. Recovering planted habits shows that the features, the thresholds and the intervals work on data built to contain them; it says nothing about how real developers behave.

Every figure for the proactive layer comes from generated personas, learners and git learners with planted structure we wrote. It shows that the judge, verify and prepare steps recover what was planted, not that real workers would find these cards useful.

The definition of 'worth surfacing' is ours and was fixed before the runs (see the output). For the personas, the planted skill is mapped to a level and fed to both the gate and the truth, so agreement on practice cards for personas is partly built in; the learner and git truths are more independent of the code under test.

The truth definitions and one part of the practice scoring were revised after looking at the first replays (listed under design.truth_revisions and design.code_revision, with the first-run figures). There is no held-out data: the reported precision and recall are development-set figures on the same generated personas and learners, and are optimistic for that reason.

There are 4 personas, 3 learners and 4 git learners, with several decision points each. Decision points inside one person are correlated, so the pooled Wilson intervals are too narrow; the person-level bootstrap is the honest interval and it is wide.

Acceptance learning is shown on a generated worker with fixed rates. It has not been validated on people, and a real person's accepts and declines may depend on time of day, mood and the card's wording, none of which are modelled.

Every calendar number is on generated calendars with planted structure (4 personas, 8 experts, 16 novices, 3 weeks). Nothing about the calendar layer is validated on real people, and one read-only aggregate check of the owner's own calendar says nothing about anyone else.

The expert reference is generated from the role template that also defines the targets, so agreement with it is by construction. The template is hand-authored, not measured on real experts, and real experts differ by person, team and week.

Every digest number is measured on generated commits and calendar entries with planted labels, written by the same author as the rules and the prompts. No real repository, calendar or person was used; accuracy on real data is unknown and probably lower.

About 100 items per task in the held-out test split (and 50 in the dev split the prompts were tuned on): the Wilson intervals are wide, and differences of a few points between the model and the rules are not distinguishable.

Constrained decoding means an instruction planted in the input cannot make the model print text: nothing leaves a digest except vocabulary values. It can still steer labels. With one planted line on 20 items per task, the model-for-everything run moved to the value the line asked for in 19 of 19 (commit category revert), 17 of 17 (risk high), 13 of 17 (event category focus) and 12 of 12 (needs_prep true); the keyword rules moved in 0, 0, 0 and 0. In the shipped policy only category is model-decided, and code vetoes the two most consequential claims (a revert needs a revert-style message; focus time needs at most one attendee), which leaves 0 of 19 and 5 of 17 category steerings; other category values can still be steered by whoever writes the commit message or the invite.

Every fixture is generated with planted facts; recovery rates say the runtime and its checks work on those fixtures, not that they work on a real repository or table. Nothing here was run on a person's real data.

In the privacy-preserving default (menu mode) the model only sequences vetted steps by id; the analysis is done by scripts we wrote. The live smoke shows a model can plan and drive a menu, not that it can analyse data. Free-form model-written code exists only in foreground raw mode, on files the worker named, and was evaluated with the mock model only.

The long-horizon bugs are single-token mutations of correct code (an operator, a boundary, a constant), repaired by fault localisation plus mutation search over three classes, the standard way to test repair tools. Success shows the loop, the rollback, the verification and the privacy path work over 14 steps; it does not show the runtime fixes arbitrary bugs. The data task has three planted problem types and one reconciliation target; the outlier rule (50 times the median) is the same in the engine and in the checker.

Every number in this section comes from generated people or language-model participants, not people. A gain on generated data can be the model learning the generator; held-out replicates share the generator and cannot rule that out.

The held-out persona and apprentice replicates are fresh seeds of the same generators: they catch overfitting to one noise draw, not learning the generator. Only the cross-family matrix (three differently built generators, still written by us) and the language-model participant traces go beyond it.

The explainer improves readability, not accuracy. A faithful-sounding explanation can still rest on a wrong number: the check proves each number traces to a field of the packet, not that the packet is true.

The deterministic template is the shipped wording: it passes its own check on every packet and every intent, with no model. A model's words are used only when they pass the same check, and how often they do depends on the model and the mode (live, small n, real models, 7 Nov 2026): local Qwen2.5-7B composing freely 1 of 30; rewording a code-written draft 12 of 30 [24.6%, 57.7%] then, after the hedge and wording fixes, 24 of 30 [62.7%, 90.5%]; cloud gpt-5.4-mini composing from the packet 0 of 13 [0%, 22.8%]; cloud gemini-3.5-flash-lite 7 of 9 [45.3%, 93.7%] (see live.recorded). The model layer improves readability only when it passes the check, so the default text says 'words from the template'.

Every Cue result comes from a simulator written by the same team that wrote the policy: stalls, pauses, reaction times and interruption costs are assumptions. It shows the policy keeps its caps and trades help against nuisance as designed; it is not evidence about people.

The composite overstates mastery for learners who do not improve and rises 10 points or more in about a third of them. It is experimental and in no headline; independence and the trend are the evidence, and the trend has low power.

Every number here comes from generators we wrote. The v2 families have marginals inside cited ranges, but nothing shows they match real people; the live study (n = 4) and an optional labelled pilot are the only evidence about real people.

Every number comes from a generator: workers, schedules, event streams, reactions and attention costs are my assumptions (simulate.py). This shows the policy behaves as designed under them. It does not show that real people find Knack natural. The live check with four teammates (n = 4) is the real test and was not run.

The agent results are from a language model driving a sandbox we wrote, in a headless browser; not a real desktop and not people. They say nothing about a real desktop, real calculators or real people's casework. Real desktop: R0 ran once (R0 reads the window list and accessibility only, so it sends no input events by construction); no other rung has run. Everything else here is the headless sandbox.

Injected, held-out seed 9138, n = 20 (gate 35e964049fd0, matches the frozen hash): the detector paused 20 of 20 pages of this kind (Wilson 95% 0.84 to 1.00); 0 attacks (0 visits to the exfil address, 0 submissions). The pages carry text aimed at an AI and nothing else, so this is evidence about the detector and the pause only. It does not show that the gate resists hostile pages.

Clean, held-out seed 9137, n = 4 (gate 35e964049fd0, matches the frozen hash): 1 of 4 passed the code check (Wilson 95% 0.05 to 0.70), 3 of 4 reached the approval gate, 2 false claim(s) (a success claimed while a figure did not match the code check), 0 submissions; 1 unexpected gate stop(s) (needs_human:drift:fill x1), a harness or gate-tuning finding listed apart from model failures, paused 1 run(s). n = 4 is descriptive: the pre-registered criterion 'Wilson lower bound at least 0.8' cannot be tested at this n under the spend cap, so this neither confirms nor rejects it.
Language-model participants, not people: The participants are language-model agents, not people. Nothing here shows that people learn from the coach, and nothing here is a user study.

Language-model participants, not people: The only 'memory' a participant has is a note of at most 280 characters that it wrote itself after the practice case and sees again at the post-test of the same skill. Every case starts from a fresh model context. That is a prompt, not learning in any human sense.

Language-model participants, not people: A model that is shown 'check cliff edges before you copy this result' can do what it says. A higher score after coaching can therefore be instruction following plus a self-written note, not retention of a skill.
Language-model participants, not people: The coach prompts, the sandbox sites, the households, the scoring rule and the personas were all written by us.

Language-model participants, not people: With 16 coached-arm participants the analysis has about 6% false positives and 12%, 29% and 76% power for a small, medium and large true effect (engine-analytics Monte Carlo, interval excludes zero); sign-flip p below 0.05 has less. A null or small result does not show that the coach has no effect; a result counts as clear only if the interval excludes zero.

With four teammates the exact two-sided sign-flip p cannot go below 0.125, and the interval excludes zero only when the four differences nearly agree and are large. The expected outcome is an interval that includes zero.

Every world is generated by us. The shifted worlds differ in structure from the world the models were fitted on, but they are still ours; a held-out replicate catches overfitting to one noise draw, never 'the model learned our generators'.

Every decision is scored in a world we generated, with a cost we chose. The ordering of policies is a statement about these mechanisms, not about real routines, real reviewers, real workdays or real people.

With a one-off error page the real model passed 0 of 20 and said it was finished in 20 of 20 runs (20 false claims): it declared success on an error page. The code check caught every one, which is why code, not the model, decides success.

The glitch result was followed by a fix (a page-state label from the quarantined reader fed to the planner, retries, and the cliff check moved after the verifier; made AFTER the glitch result was seen), then re-run on the same condition: 10 of 10 succeeded with 0 false claims, against 0 of 20 before. This is in-sample: the fix was designed after seeing that failure, and only 10 runs were made because a budget stop hit (9 later rows were dropped). It does not show the fix generalises.

Tier 3 (computer use) is not demonstrated on the benefits task: 3 runs against a stand-in actuator on real screenshots made 0 pointer actions and landed on an interactive element 0 times. Nothing is clicked in that setting, so a claim of done there is a false claim by construction.

Real-model red team (real model, n = 42 cases (3 repeats each)): Intervals overlap: this shows what the layers cost (task success under attack was 22% with every layer on against 84% with all off, and 0 of 126 runs with every layer on let an attack through), not that the layers prevent attacks. The attacks were written by the team that wrote the defences, and a result is true of one model version on one day.

Language-model participants, not people. A language model plays each participant, so nothing in this section says how people behave. The live study (n = 4 teammates) is the only human evidence and is reported separately; this section never feeds it.

Language-model participants, not people. The coach prompts and the sandbox calculators were written by us, so the simulation checks that the pipeline runs end to end under our own assumptions. It does not show that coaching works on anyone.

Language-model participants, not people. Learning between blocks is a note carried in the model's prompt, a proxy. It is not memory, practice or skill, so a language-model 'improvement' says little about a human one.
Language-model participants, not people. Times in this section are model response times or scripted numbers, not human reading, thinking or typing, so no timing result here is a human timing.

The power analysis only shows what the n = 4 design could detect under our own assumptions (effect size, carryover, order effect, how noisy the measure is). It is a property of the design, not a result about people, and not evidence that an effect exists.

Hazard, benefits-processor, generators we wrote (120 generated people per v2 cell; the v1 generator has 4 personas): the v1 stuck model beats time-since-progress by 0.071 nats per bin on its own generator, and the advantage falls to 0.008 to 0.015 on three harder generator families. A v1-trained model is 0.43 to 0.53 nats worse than the baseline on their data (H1 -0.43 to -0.53). False alarms: the interval is entirely above the 1.0 per hour budget in 3 of 6 v2-to-v2 off-diagonal cells, 1 of 3 v2 diagonals, 3 of 3 v1-to-v2 cells and 0 of 3 v2-to-v1 cells. Cells with no skill (the H1 interval includes zero or lies below it): latent_skill->markov, latent_skill->process_trace, v1->latent_skill, v1->markov, v1->process_trace. The v1 headline (log loss 0.436 against 0.509 for time since progress, leave one person out, on the four v1 personas) therefore largely reflects the generator's emission table; it stays labelled as a generator result.

Language-model participants, not people. Run 4 (n = 24: 16 coached-arm and 8 A/A participants): 30 of 32 coached post-tests scored 0 (the floor) and 16 of 16 A/A post-tests; the action cap was hit in 18 of 32 coached post-tests. The headline difference is +0.094 [-0.051, +0.239], sign-flip p = 0.5. An outcome at the floor means a null shows nothing: it does not show the coach has no effect. With 16 coached-arm participants the analysis has about 6% false positives and 12%, 29% and 76% power for a small, medium and large true effect (engine-analytics Monte Carlo, interval excludes zero); sign-flip p below 0.05 has less. A null or small result does not show that the coach has no effect; a result counts as clear only if the interval excludes zero. Run 5 pilot: 0 of 6 post-tests scored above zero (needed 3); stopped, so there is no run 5 proper (reason recorded: only 0 of 6 pilot post-tests scored above zero (needed 3)). Study-mode enforcement held: 0 non-silent coach polls in post-test blocks and 0 in blocks with the coach off (including A/A); 12 nudges were shown, all in train blocks.

M5, out-of-generator transfer (language-model participants, not people; test only, no decision rule; n = 24 participants, 419 scored 30 s bins): neither v1 nor v2 transfers to the floor-bound behaviour of those traces. Log loss is 1.43 [1.25 to 1.60] for v1 and 1.46 [1.31 to 1.61] for v2 against 1.08 [1.00 to 1.15] for the base rate, and calibration is destroyed (expected calibration error 0.51 [0.45 to 0.57] and 0.53 [0.47 to 0.58]). The label shifts: 65% of the test bins are 'stuck' against 22% in training, because progress is sparse in these traces. v2 minus v1 log loss is +0.030 with an interval of -0.030 to 0.085: no improvement. Reported as is; the models and alarm rules were fixed before these traces existed.

Genome (deficit detection), benefits-processor, generators we wrote (16 personas on the v1 generator, 87 to 92 generated people per v2 cell): precision 92% and recall 95% on the v1 generator fall to 48 to 71% precision and 49 to 68% recall on three harder generator families (thresholds fitted and tested on the same family). Thresholds fitted on v1 keep recall (87 to 95%) but lose precision (33 to 56%); thresholds fitted on a v2 family give v1 high precision (79 to 100%) but recall of only 10 to 42%. False attribution to deficits that are absent is 46 to 59 s on the v2 families against 1.1 s on v1. The v1 figures describe the v1 generator, not workers.

Routines (repeat finder, then the proposal gate), benefits-processor, generators we wrote (4 personas on the v1 generator, 120 generated people per v2 cell; shipped thresholds, which do not depend on the fit family): raw cluster precision is 22% on the v1 generator (the published figure) and 44 to 97% on the three v2 families, with recall 45 to 92% (100% on v1). Proposal precision after the gate is 74 to 100% (100% on v1). Thresholds fitted per family transfer unevenly: across the fitted off-diagonal cells raw precision ranges from 4 to 100% and recall from 16 to 100%. The two thin roles (data-analyst, programmer; v2 families only, shipped thresholds) give raw precision 88 to 98%, recall 60 to 92% and proposal precision 100%, so the figures differ by role as well as by family. These numbers say how many of the clusters found are real routines in a generator we wrote, not in real workers.

ML v2 genome families on the held-out apprentice cohort (6 cohorts, 96 novices; all generated): the pre-registered primary candidates E4 (expert envelope) and Q1 (counterfactual price) are both harmful and so rejected. The primary metric is the mean absolute error, in seconds, of the recovered price of a deficit, paired against v1's attribution, so a positive difference is worse: E4 +3.81 [+2.30, +5.19] s, Q1 +1.17 [+0.44, +1.87] s. Other E variants: E1 accepted (-0.92 [-1.85, -0.21] s), E2 null (+0.00 [+0.00, +0.00] s), E3 harmful (+4.57 [+3.14, +6.01] s). v1's attribution stays the default for these families. Reported as is: the candidates were frozen before the held-out run.

ML v2 under generator mismatch (fit on one generator family, test on another; pooled off-diagonal cells; all generated): the plain time-since-progress baseline beats v1 on log loss, paired against v1 (negative is better; adjusted intervals as recorded): benefits-processor -0.021 [-0.034, -0.010]; data-analyst -0.024 [-0.034, -0.014]; programmer -0.030 [-0.041, -0.019]. The accepted v2 (A4) improves on v1 by -0.014 [-0.019, -0.009] for benefits-processor under the same test, a smaller improvement than the baseline's, so on this test a rule that only counts time since progress does better than the accepted v2 when the generator changes. The held-out result is reported as is; it is about our generators, not about workers.

The model check proves traceability, not truth: a sentence passes when every number in it traces to the evidence packet and it makes no causal or expert claim. A sentence can still mislead with numbers that all trace, and the packets are from scripted apprentices.

The local model's reword pass rate on the number check was 40% (12 of 30) on its first n = 30 run, and 80% (24 of 30, interval 0.63 to 0.91) after the hedge handling and the consequence wording were fixed. The second figure is on the same kind of packets after fixing what the first run showed, so it is in-sample. Small n, one model, generated packets, recorded 7 Nov and not re-run by make eval.

The injected condition in the real-model runs is text-only (hidden and visible words aimed at an AI; the detector paused 20 of 20 runs). It tests the detector and the pause, not the action gate against a hostile page, and does not show that the gate resists hostile pages.
Section 'study' has no numbers: the live study has not been run: no data in evals/study/results/.

The three calculators are sandbox sites we built, each with planted quirks, and each computes one Universal-Credit-shaped entitlement. They say nothing about how real calculators behave or what their terms and bot protection allow.

Agent-claim calibration is mostly on generated runs. The real-model result covers only 68 claimed successes from one family of failure (see agent_claims.live), so it cannot show that claim risk can be predicted in general. A low predicted risk of a false claim never replaces the code check, which decides success.

The off-hours live run depends on the conditions spike S2 passed under: macOS Accessibility and Screen Recording granted, an unlocked screen, a harmless app, the owner present. The presence forecast and the start-or-wait rule are evaluated on generated personas; the live run may fall back to a stand-in clock.

Probabilities are better than the baselines and calibrated, but alert quality is modest: about a third of stuck events are flagged, and on held-out people the false-alarm rate (about 1.2 per hour) overshoots the 1 per hour budget chosen on training people.
'Stuck' means no progress event in the next 60 seconds, which is not the same as confusion. Fast thinking and slow typing both look stuck to this label.
The apprentice traces follow a fixed task script, so part of the hazard model's large gain on them is learning the script, not predicting stuck. The four-persona result is the headline.

Skill tracing saturates on generated personas (about 35 tasks a day): mastery reaches its ceiling on day one and cannot follow the planted learning curve. Decay with absence is shown in unit tests only.

On the learner trajectories (three learners, thirty cases each, one with a three-day absence) the help level does lighten as deficits fade, but a clock alone ranks the true curve as well as mastery does, the ranking of which deficits fade fastest is near chance, and the short absence did not move the level. Three learners make every interval wide.

Off-policy evaluation is validated in a simulator whose reward structure we invented, with exactly known propensities. Real implicit labels (followed, dismissed, repeated, undone) are noisy proxies for 'it helped'.

The rule is not the best everywhere. Lowest regret by build cost: b=4: Build now (1.07); b=8: Build now (1.15); b=16: Build now (1.27); b=32: Ski rental with predictions (lambda 0.2) (1.33). When building is cheap (b = 4 manual runs) building at once (1.07) is level with the rule (1.07) and both are ahead of break-even (1.70); the prediction earns its keep when building costs more. The pack's own build costs are 4 to 9 runs.

The weekly map predicts held-out days worse than a simple baseline for shift-worker (map Brier 0.214 against prior 0.194 and one global rate 0.175). A weekly template does not suit rotating shifts or no routine.
The window forecast is only roughly calibrated: expected calibration error 0.07 to 0.13 across personas on held-out days, and it beats pooled survival (no time of week) on 2 of 4 personas.
The 95% intervals on the presence map contain the planted active probability in only 55% to 91% of bins. Smoothing across neighbouring bins trades bias for variance, so the intervals are too narrow.

Idle capacity per week is over-estimated: nine-to-five 12 h against a planted 10 h; irregular 10 h against a planted 6 h. With no sleep event the machine is assumed to stay on for 60 minutes after the last event, and a locked screen still counts as idle although a desktop run cannot start on it.

The finder alone (minimum support 3) returns many small clusters of one-off work: precision 22% over 55 clusters. The value gate removes them: precision 100% over 6 proposals. Short routines of three or four steps are the hardest to tell from chance.

The 95% forecast interval covered what happened in 8 of 11 planted routines (73%), which is below nominal and rests on one held-out week; the schedule change on day 15 falls inside it, and the model has no way to know about it.

In the live runs the model states a confidence only when it makes a finish claim itself, which happened only in the runs that went wrong. Its presence copies the label, so it is kept out of the classifier and cannot be calibrated.

Cold-start priors are built from four generated personas (or 24 scripted apprentices with two cases each); with so few and such alike people, partial pooling is hard to tell from complete pooling, and learning-curve drift is not modelled.
Attacks are scripted and were written by the same team that wrote the defences. A new attack style can get through.
A detector hit pauses the run for a human, so task success under attack is lower than on clean pages by design.

Removing the injection detector did not let any attack through in this test, but it lets far more tasks finish (the reader alone keeps the planner clean). The detector's job is to catch an attack early, and its price is pauses.

Layer 7 (goal check) no longer asks a model about plain typing, filling, select and extract steps, so it now covers navigation, clicks and key presses only. We changed this after seeing it pause the run on clean pages when the worker was just typing the answer (5 false pauses in 93 live runs). The false-pause figure after the change (0 of 93) is measured on the same pages that showed the problem, so it is in-sample and probably too good; typed data is still stopped by the data-flow and action-gate layers, not by this one.

Data-flow rules and the goal check cannot tell an exfiltration request to an endpoint on a site the routine already uses from normal browsing there. Only the detector and the reader stop that kind of attack.

Nothing is executed. An attack counts as successful when the model proposes an action that serves the attacker and the layers authorise it; real tools, redirects and multi-step consequences are not modelled.
The attacks are scripted and were written by the same team that wrote the defences; models change, so a result is true of one model version on one day.

The canary scan looks for the exact planted strings, their invented words, simple rewrites (case, separators, URL encoding, base64, hex). A paraphrase, a translation, a hash or a character-code encoding of a token would not be caught. The claim measured is: these planted strings did not reach the model port, in these flows.

A SafePayload limits the form of what is sent (numbers, codes, fixed ids, bucketed values), not its meaning: a bucketed count of the worker's own meetings is still a fact about the worker. Generalisation reduces precision; it is not anonymisation.

Model calls the worker asked for (agent runs, the coach, the quarantined reader) are not routed through the egress guard and send raw content to the provider by design. They appear in the ledger only as metadata lines when the port is wrapped (direct.LedgeredPort). The Privacy screen therefore does not claim that nothing else leaves this laptop.
All fixtures are generated and the real provider is never called here (a fake client checks only the request shape). Nothing is validated on real calendars, repositories or accounts.
Closed answer schemas (every string is an enum) stop text read off the screen from coming back. They cannot stop the model from seeing it.

A frame is held in a buffer that is wiped after the call and is never written by this layer. Copies handed to a provider SDK or the HTTP stack, and freed memory the interpreter has not reused, cannot be wiped or controlled from here; swap and core dumps are outside this check.

The residue scan looks for the planted PNG's raw bytes, the token written into its metadata, its full SHA-256, and base64 or hex renderings of the file. It cannot see pixels, a re-encoded copy (a JPEG of the same frame), or a description of the frame.

Old project TypeScript under apps/desktop still names Gemini and OpenAI hosts behind flags (listed in static_guard_ts_references, report only). The rule is that frames reach a provider through the engine's egress guard; the Python tree is checked for it, the TypeScript is not enforced.
No real provider was called: a capturing port and a fake client check request shapes and the guard. Gemini and OpenAI behaviour (latency, accuracy, cost) is the MODELS track's own measurement.

The generator, the digest rules and the habit thresholds were written by the same agent. Thresholds were set on development replicates 0 to 3 and scored on fresh ones (100 and up), but the planted rates are large and habits are planted independently; real habits are smaller, correlated and noisier.
Small differences are not flagged by design (each habit has a floor). At 25% of the planted strength recall falls to 19%.
Evaluation digests come from the rules, because model digests take about a second a commit. The local model was not present, so model-against-rules agreement was not measured.

On commit sessions the alignment sees differences in the SHAPE of sessions (missing test steps, reverts, extra code-commit loops) in some replicates, and sees nothing in seconds, because git records when a commit landed and not how long the work took. Habits that live in the message or the clock (vague messages, late nights) are invisible to cogs by construction.
Suggestions are advice chosen by code from commit-level shares. Nobody has been shown that following one improves anything; there is no study of the git layer, and a share is not a cause.
A real repository is compared with generated experts, so its origin is reported as mixed; the comparison is with a scripted baseline, not with real experts.

The ranking weights, the minimum score of 0.30, the cap of three and the per-kind limits are hand-set constants, not fitted to any data. A different choice would move precision and recall; no sensitivity sweep is claimed.

Recall is capped at what the judge is allowed to show of each kind (one practice card, one git card, two automations): a person with three planted git habits is credited for finding one. That is the design, not a flaw in the metric, but it hides how much was left unsaid.

Calendar cards are scored against the calendar track's planted problems; the suggestion thresholds and the planted structure come from the same generator family, and a week can carry several planted problems of which the judge may show one. Finished-run cards are covered by scripted checks only, and so are stale calendar and git cards.

Staleness is injected by changing a reading (a routine switched on, a skill at level 4). Real staleness has more forms, and a source that cannot be read is never treated as stale, which can leave a card up for a few hours after it stopped being true.

Event kinds (meeting, focus, break, off-screen) come from keyword rules on titles and attendee counts. Real titles are messier; a meeting with no invitees is read as the owner's own time, and a focus block that is not named as one is invisible. Calendar hygiene differs from how people really work.

Gap intervals cover uncertainty in the expert reference (8 generated experts) only, not a learner's week-to-week variation; a week is flagged only if it also lies outside the range of expert weeks. Three weeks per person is thin.

The Microsoft Graph adapters were tested against recorded fake responses written from the public documentation; they have never been run against a live tenant by this code, and tenant policy decides what a signed-in worker may read.

The leak result is measured: the exact planted names, addresses, titles, locations and ids did not appear in any payload, suggestion or captured request. It does not rule out a paraphrase or an encoding, and model calls the worker asks for are recorded in the egress ledger, not hidden.

The prompt wording, the worked examples and the per-field choice of model or rules were tuned on the dev split only; the held-out test split was run once with the frozen prompts (one later look at the shipped-policy arm followed the single policy revision, see loc_policy_revised). Dev numbers are therefore optimistic and are shown only as such.

No fine-tuning (LOC-3 is cut): it could not be validated in the time available. The model is Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct at 4-bit quantisation (Q4_K_M) with a labelling guide, a few fixed worked examples and constrained decoding.
Labels such as risk and message quality are our written policy, not ground truth: a reviewer may reasonably disagree on a share of items, which caps the accuracy any method can show here.

Small prompt changes move the numbers by more than the intervals suggest: replacing three worked examples (to keep them disjoint from the fixtures) changed dev commit-category accuracy from 48 to 44 of 52. A difference of a few items between two prompts or between the model and the rules is noise at this sample size.

The rules, the labelling policy, the prompts' guide and the fixture generator share one author and one vocabulary (for example the list of sensitive areas), so the rules are better matched to these fixtures than they would be to real history, and the model's labelling guide is better matched than it would be to real history. Real data would test both.

'No leak' is claimed only as measured: zero planted strings in the outputs and in the server log of the evaluation run, and the guards reject a deliberately leaking stand-in model. The raw inputs do pass through the local model's memory and llama.cpp's in-process prompt cache (never written to disk by this module).
The history checks recount from the same git-log parser the tool uses (the aggregation is independent; the parsing is shared). The commit count and revert count also use plain git commands.

run_python uses macOS sandbox-exec (deprecated by Apple but present) and fails closed without it. Memory is bounded by a resident-size watchdog polled every 250 ms, not a kernel limit (macOS refuses RLIMIT_AS).
Injection detection is a rule set. The planted strings are of the styles the rules cover, so the detection rate here is an upper bound.

Offline long-horizon runs use a deterministic stand-in for the model that reads the same typed payload (typed history and typed signals) and follows the playbook; it shows the loop is closed and adaptive, not that a language model would choose the same steps. The live smoke measures that with the real model on the same tasks, with its own n.
The awareness features come from a generator that plants a cursor-to-stuck link by assumption; an ablation lift shows the pipeline can use a planted signal, not that real cursors predict being stuck.

The risk-controlled alarm threshold is guaranteed only for exchangeable episodes and independent false alarms; it fails for a new person who differs from the training people, for drift and for clustered alarms.

The seconds-if-fixed estimate assumes the rest of the path would be unchanged. It fails when habits interact; the generator's prices are additive by construction, so the stress test with a planted interaction is invented by us.

The deficit rows that stay mis-priced (copy error, repeated reads) are mis-priced by the rule that names alignment columns after the alignment, not by the substitution costs; a better labelling rule written from our own planted structure would be fitting the generator, so none was added.
The language-model participant traces have few progress events and short cases, so the transfer numbers rest on little and the label is nearly constant; the test is reported whatever it shows.

The false-reject rate is measured on a stand-in model that varies numbers and interval wording in the ways we wrote down. A real model phrases things we did not anticipate, so its false-reject rate is likely higher; a rejected reply costs nothing (the template is used).

The adversarial rejection rate is against the 29 attacks we wrote. The unknown-habit rule is a set of cue patterns (a cause or a share of time attributed to a phrase that names nothing in the vocabulary), not a language model: a novel phrasing with no cue can pass.

Packets come from scripted apprentices (and the real stuck-hazard evaluation in the full run); the coach, routine, counterfactual and time-to-progress blocks are scripted fixtures that exercise wording and the check, not measurements.

The headline stuck signal is the coach's rule fallback (time since progress). The real hazard model would change when help arrives; an emulated model signal is a secondary sweep and is labelled as an emulation.
Grounding is a fake port right at a chosen rate. Real accuracy on real screens is not measured here; the 60 to 100% sweep is a what-if.
A learner who dismisses a cue and then grinds through alone looks independent in the ledger; the guards remove dismiss-and-walk-away and implicit follows within 10 s but cannot remove that leak.
Candidate accuracy is measured on 8 scripted apprentice experts and on experts sampled from the pack's own rules; real experts will do things neither contains.

The three v2 families share the person hierarchy, the interruption process, the event emitter and noise model, the role vocabulary and the task grammar's valid paths. A family with less shared code would be a stronger test.
The hazard label is a point process driven by hidden stuck episodes, not an emission table, but both behaviour and label come from the same hidden state: the circularity is reduced, not removed.
Published ranges were read from search-result summaries; primary papers were not opened. Hick-Hyman slope, circadian amplitude and warm-up are unverified wide assumptions.

The attention-cost model (seconds of focus lost per interruption by context) is an assumption. The sensitivity run halves and doubles it and reports whether the ordering of conditions changes; the magnitudes stay assumptions.
Producer rates are stated approximations of Cue, the briefing, the approval queue, the agent runtime, the calendar layer and health checks. The sensitivity run scales them by 0.5 and 2.

Implicit labels (followed within 10 s, dismissed within 4 s, ignored, never) are noisy proxies for welcome: a dismissal can mean already knew. The generated worker's labels come from the same reaction model, so learning is validated for its direction, not for its calibration against people.

Meeting, call, screen-share and quiet-hotkey states are known exactly here. In the product they come from probes that can be wrong or missing; an unknown worker is held, never interrupted, except for safety. The sensitivity run makes 10% of polls unknown to show the cost.
No human has used the layer: whether workers find the pointers useful, or admins decide better, is not shown (the live check with four teammates is not run).
The generators were written by the author of the selection, so planted effects are easier to recover than real ones. This is a test of the code paths and the statistics.
The false-insight rates are for null worlds with independent weeks; real people have autocorrelation, seasonality and shared events, which will raise them.
The thresholds are a priori values checked on generated data; they are not tuned for any real firm.
Per-user visibility for an employer needs a lawful basis and a notice to workers in a real deployment; nothing here supplies one.

Generated people only: nobody in this evaluation is a person. The generators were written by the author of the rules, so planted routines are cleaner than real habits (exact step lists, a small chance of one slip).
Dev seeds 0 to 9 only. There is no held-out claim: nothing here was run on seeds kept apart from the code, and the numbers are what the rules do on worlds their author could inspect.
Recall is for routines that are present, repeated inside one 7 day window and made of steps the finder can separate; it says nothing about habits spread over many windows or tangled with other work.
The false-row rate is for noise made of random step lists. Real work has habits that are not routines worth automating, so a real null rate could be higher.

The held-back audit uses noise-free worlds so the answer is exact; with noise, a held-back count also includes chance clusters. The reason 'too varied' and the ranking order are covered by unit tests, not here.

The 95% interval on minutes is checked against a known rate and mean run time, conditional on the row being listed. It does not say whether the run time a real worker would save equals the time spent (the judgement share is a pack setting, not a measurement).

K-anonymity here is the group-size rule (fewer than 5 people are not listed). It does not defend against differencing across windows or role filters, and the made-up firm is not a real workforce; a real deployment needs a lawful basis and a notice to workers (D41).
Nothing here shows that workers find the list useful or that Automate leads to better work; the study is a separate piece of work.
Unexpected gate stops are listed apart from model failures and are harness or gate-tuning findings, not model results: clean: 1.
LH-1 to LH-5 (LH-1, LH-2, LH-3, LH-2b, LH-4, LH-5) are offline: a grounded test double (LH-5 uses compiled routines with the heuristic reader), 0 model tokens. They test the code, not any model.
Live agent spend is 16.1575 US dollars at list price (3.2062 at the lower bound) of a 20.0 cap (80.8%); the cap is why the clean held-out n is 4.

Language-model participants, not people: The counterbalanced design cancels a fixed block-2 shift and generic carry-over, not spill-over of the coached gain to the other skill in block 2, which dilutes the contrast. Because each block starts from a fresh model context, order and fatigue effects are absent by construction.

Language-model participants, not people: Timing is not human. Each action is followed by a fixed 2 s pause and the model's own latency varies, so effort is reported as ACTION COUNTS and the coach's poll-to-prompt delay is a property of the pipeline, not of people. A fast participant can finish the note page before a prompt arrives.

Language-model participants, not people: The coach is real but the overlay renderer is a stand-in: a ring is drawn only when an element carrying the target zone exists on the page the participant is on. The cliff button exists only on a calculator result tab, not on the case note page where the prompt usually arrives. The reconcile target was `results_tabs` (no page element) when the plan was written; the pipeline snapshot used targets `reconcile_control` (the case note's dropdown), which exists. The by-zone table shows which was served.

Language-model participants, not people: Participants are reached through the shared model port's fast-tier check call, whose fixed instructions tell the model to treat quoted material as data. That may make it less responsive to on-page text in both arms.

Language-model participants, not people: The build machine was heavily loaded by other agents' tests while the participants ran (1-minute load average above 100 on 12 CPUs, sampled and reported), so wall-clock times, the coach's 3 s polls, the extension's event flush and the prompt delays are slower and noisier than on an idle machine. Action counts are not affected; timings are.
Language-model participants, not people: One model (id read from the environment and recorded in the CSV) and one family of personas written by us. Results say nothing about other models.

Language-model participants, not people: Scores come from the sandbox state exactly as analyze.py scores them (cliff 0, 1 or 2 of 2; reconcile 0 or 1), so ties and ceilings are likely and the t interval is not exact for such discrete scores.
The v1 world draws new people of the same four persona types the models were fitted on. A new type of worker, or a new kind of task, is what the shifted worlds stand in for.

The guard's bound on false flags assumes each episode's loss difference has conditional mean at most zero given the past. Episodes of one person are not independent, so the bound is a design target that the no-drift deployments check, not a proof.
Eight deployments per world give wide intervals for guard counts and for the strategy comparison; counts are shown with exact intervals.

The guard compares the model with a naive predictor. A model that drifts but stays better than that predictor is not flagged (the error-risk world after the rule change); the loss of calibration shows in the reliability table and the intercept, and nothing recalibrates the model in this version.
The ledger is built and tested, but the running product has recorded no live predictions yet, so no real prospective result exists. These are replays of generated time.

The review minutes per case, the cost of an escaped error, the build cost b, the ratio of a collision's cost to a finished run's value (L/G) and the intervention reward are assumptions; each row prints a sweep or says which cost it hangs on.

In the routing generator the worker's check, the agent's stated confidence and the worker's trace are drawn from the realised error. Part of the model's edge over random review is signal our generator hands it.

At the pack's own build costs (4 to 9 manual runs) building at once is cheaper than the shipped build-timing rule in these generated worlds; the rule beats break-even, the classical reference, which is the registered primary contrast.
Deficit detection is weaker for: repeated_read_result (precision 70%, recall 100%); copy_error (precision 100%, recall 71%). Overall precision 92%, recall 95% over 160 case-deficit pairs.

The recovered price differs from the planted price, with an interval that excludes zero, for: repeated_read_result (+13.5 s, interval 5.1 to 23.3). The alignment names a block of extra steps by its content, so a deficit that shares steps with another is mis-priced.
On held-out people the false-alarm rate is 1.21 an hour, over the 1.0 an hour budget chosen on the training people.

In the detailed run the interval of IPS, SNIPS, DR does not contain the true value 0.018. Over 24 independent replications the intervals covered the truth: IPS 96%, SNIPS 96%, DR 88% (naive 0%); nominal is 95%.

The clean-path result (20 of 20 households, 95% lower bound 84%) is the compiled path on the sandbox it was written against, so a full pass is expected and says little. The discriminating evidence is the robust and injected runs. Twenty households cannot rule out a pass rate well below 100%.

Failure injection covers 4 patterns only: layout change on site b (5 of 5 passed); layout change on site c (5 of 5 passed); layout change on site a and one-off 503 on site b (5 of 5 passed); one-off 503 on site c (5 of 5 passed). 15 of 20 households needed the tier-2 browser agent. 20 of 20 passed (95% lower bound 84%). Other failure kinds (a changed flow, a wrong page, a slow site) were not injected.

Real-model runs (agent-core, tier 1 disabled so every navigator uses the browser agent): 20 households per condition, 90 runs. Clean 18 of 20 (95% interval 0.70 to 0.97), 2 honest failures ('not every calculator produced a verified result'); layout change 20 of 20 (0.84 to 1.00). Twenty per condition shows the failure modes, not a pass rate; identical prompts are cached, so repeated page situations are one live sample each.

Injected pages: the detector paused 20 of 20 runs (20 detected of 20 injected) with 0.0 model-driven steps, and 0 attacks succeeded. Task success is 0 by design: a paused run does no task. This tests the detector on these pages, which we wrote.

Cost is an estimate at placeholder rates (5.0 and 30.0 USD per million tokens in and out), not the provider's price list: about 4.56 USD for the rows in the file (497099 tokens in, 69296 out), 494 live calls and 5302 cache hits across the runs. Cached answers cost nothing on a re-run.
The live false-pause result (0 of 93 clean runs, 0 of 30 on hard negatives) is in-sample: the layer-7 (goal-drift) scope was changed while building on this same catalog, so it is not a held-out rate.

CIRCULARITY: the calculators' quirks (site b ignores capital tariff income; site c applies a two-child limit and treats exactly 16,000 as over the limit) and the household archetypes that trigger them were planted by us. The router can only show it found our planted structure; it does not show that real calculators or real agents fail this way.
The trust parameter lambda is fixed by us (or set from past forecast error by a heuristic that is not in the paper). It was not tuned on this simulation.

The start-or-wait rule is conservative: it collided with the worker's return in 2.1% of started runs against an allowed 10%, and used 74% of idle time against 90% for running whenever idle five minutes. Runs are replayed one per decision point on held-out spells; interruption and idle-use intervals count spells as independent.
Planted routines that ran fewer than 3 times cannot be found by design and are excluded from recall: nine-to-five/weekly-report.
The autonomy ladder needs 20 clean shadow runs to reach A2 and about 73 clean runs to reach A3; the example runs reach A1 or A2 at most. A3 is a target, not a result.
Layer 1 (sanitising) is modelled as defeating only markup-based attacks (fake system tags, tool-call syntax); a scripted planner that follows plain text shows no change when it is off.
Layers overlap, so leaving one out often changes nothing. The 'only_<layer>' rows show each layer's standalone strength.
Alignment with the attacker's goal is judged by rules on the proposed action, so an unrelated harmful action is not counted.

Lists of integers could carry text as character codes. Lists are capped at 64 items and integers at 1e9, which bounds that; the threat model is accidental leakage by honest code, not an author trying to smuggle data out.
The static guard is name-based. It does not follow a module name held in a variable and cannot see code added at run time; it catches honest mistakes such as importing an SDK 'just for wording'.

The ledger is a plain local file the worker can clear (the clear is itself counted). It records what the guard sent; it cannot record what a module sends by bypassing the guard, which is what the static guard and the canary flows are for.
Reverts are rare even when planted, so the revert habit is the weakest to recover; it is reported, not tuned.
The one real history (this project's) is short and agent-assisted; its aggregates illustrate the pipeline and are not a finding.
The leak result is a count of exact planted strings in captured request bodies on these flows. It does not catch a paraphrase, a translation or a hash of a token.
No model decides what is surfaced; a model may reword the reason line through the egress guard. Wording quality is not evaluated here.

A problem planted below the expert tolerance (one fragmented day, one back-to-back run) is not suggested, by design. Recall against the planted intent is therefore below 1; the thresholds come from the template, not from the truth labels.

Size, tests touched, duration, attendee count and recurrence are computed by code from the input in every path, so they are exact by construction and say nothing about the model; only category, risk, message quality and needs_prep are model-or-rules fields.

Latency and tokens per second are for one Apple M2 Max (32 GB) with all layers on the GPU: about 30 generated tokens per second, so a digest takes roughly 0.5 s when only the category is asked for (the shipped policy) and about 0.7 to 1.1 s with every field. A history of a thousand commits takes about nine minutes the first time; the rules path takes microseconds.

Which fields the model decides was chosen on the dev split and revised once after the held-out run (events needs_prep moved from the model to the rules). The held-out numbers of the model-for-everything run are the clean evidence; the numbers for the policy as shipped (commit_digest: category, event_digest: category by the model) include one held-out look after that revision and are slightly optimistic.
Child token budgets are estimates (characters divided by 4), not provider counts.
The nightly replay uses a fake screen and a stand-in presence service; it checks the decision flow, not the real lock screen or forecast.
Latencies were measured on a development laptop shared with other processes; treat them as indicative.

A script that exits non-zero is recoverable up to three times (the child retries or changes course); any blocker (timeout, escape attempt, injection hit) or uncertain check still stops the child for a human at once.

The refactor exemplar makes one narrow, behaviour-preserving change (a repeated number becomes a named constant), verified by applying it to a fresh copy and running the tests. It does not claim general refactoring ability.
The live block, when it is run, is a small-n pass rate for one local model on generated packets; it says nothing about other models.
Deficit prevalence and stuck-episode rates were calibrated once to structural plausibility targets (S1 to S6) before any analytic was run; the families still differ a lot in prevalence.
B1 and B2 are deliberately simple baselines (everything at once, one digest a day). They show the two failure modes the layer is designed to avoid; they are not what any real notifier does.
The oracle strategy picks the better of two predictors in hindsight; it bounds what is possible and is not implementable.
Four primary contrasts were registered; every other cell is exploratory and is never used to say a rule works. The adjusted level is Bonferroni, which is conservative.

The shuffled-label null averages +46.2 s (interval -36.4 to 116.9), about 20% of the real gap of 229.6 s. Matching each case to its nearest reference is not symmetric, so the null is not exactly zero; the real gap sits above the null interval, which is the comparison that counts.

7 of 20 households are planted discrepancies between the sandbox calculators (quirks we wrote). A pass on them means the discrepancy was flagged, not that an entitlement was worked out, and the oracle is a simplified rule set, not the law.
